status: DIRECTIONAL REFERENCE — NOT A CLINICAL DECISION TOOL
disclaimer: Compiled from the FDA Prograf prescribing information and published pharmacokinetic literature. Agent PK uses this list only to say which DIRECTION a level is likely to move and to trigger a human review. It never estimates a magnitude, never adjusts a dose, and never substitutes for the transplant team's own interaction check.

direction_key.raises: Reduces clearance or increases absorption. Tacrolimus level goes UP. Toxicity risk.
direction_key.lowers: Increases clearance. Tacrolimus level goes DOWN. Rejection risk.
direction_key.additive_harm: Does not move the tacrolimus level; adds its own harm on top.

entries.mechanism: CYP3A (and P-gp) inhibitor; magnitude strongly dose- and route-dependent
entries.strength: variable: negligible at prophylactic dose, strong at treatment dose
entries.note: THE DEMO CASE, chosen deliberately. The azole most likely to be added by a prescriber who is not the transplant team: routine prophylaxis for 2-3 months post-transplant, then ordinary community prescribing for candidiasis. Its own evidence base is the clearest demonstration of why this table gives a DIRECTION and never a magnitude - the same drug spans no detectable effect at 50 mg/day to a 9.1-fold rise at treatment dose. Among the azoles it is the WEAKEST inhibitor, so it is the conservative example, not the dramatic one.
The label records a rapid, sharp rise even after a pre-emptive tacrolimus dose reduction.
Sometimes used deliberately to reduce tacrolimus dose requirement. Deliberate is not the same as unnoticed.
Effect reported to differ by CYP3A5 genotype in Chinese renal transplant patients.
One of the fastest and largest downward moves. Directly relevant where TB treatment is common.
Bought without a prescription, so it never appears on a medication list unless someone asks.
Sold over the counter. The most likely thing a patient takes without telling anyone.
Not given together; the label directs a washout between them.

foods.note: The label distinguishes single-strength juice as a moderate CYP3A inhibitor from double-strength as a strong one. Patients are told to avoid it entirely.

foods.mechanism: CYP3A inhibition, same furanocoumarin family as grapefruit
foods.note: Widely eaten in Hong Kong and southern China, and rarely thought of as a drug.

foods.mechanism: CYP3A inhibition; also independently nephrotoxic in renal impairment
reduced rate and extent of absorption
foods.note: The real risk is inconsistency. Taking it with food one week and without the next moves exposure with no dose change.

physiological_events.mechanism: damage to intestinal epithelium reduces gut CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux, so more drug is absorbed
physiological_events.note: Counterintuitive and frequently missed. Patients assume a stomach bug means they absorbed less. The opposite is documented.

physiological_events.event: vomiting within one hour of a dose
physiological_events.note: Invisible to a pill count. The tablet is gone from the box either way.

physiological_events.mechanism: tacrolimus binds extensively to erythrocytes, so whole-blood concentration shifts with haematocrit
physiological_events.note: Haematocrit is a retained covariate in most published population PK models.

He J, Yu Y, Yin C, et al. Clinically significant drug-drug interaction between tacrolimus and fluconazole in stable renal transplant recipient and literature review. J Clin Pharm Ther 2020;45(2):264-269. PMID 31756280. Treatment dose for Candida albicans oesophagitis: 9.1-fold rise in dose-normalised trough, 87% dose reduction required, still 26% lower 161 days after stopping; oral affected more than intravenous. SINGLE CASE REPORT plus review - cited for the range the literature spans, never as an expected value for any patient.
